title: The Learning Web
subject: ICT
description: Covers using Scratch to animate the story of the crafty crane and the clever crab, drawing and colouring fraction shapes with the pen tool, and building a digital plant simulation (with variables, growth stages, watering/sunlight care, and a message-triggered butterfly).

questions.question: What is Scratch?
options: A special computer program used to create animations
questions.explanation: Scratch is described in the book as 'a special computer program that helps us create animations' -- it lets you bring story characters to life on the screen.

questions.question: In Scratch, what are the characters called?
questions.explanation: Characters in Scratch are called sprites -- they act like digital puppets that we can control with code blocks.

questions.question: Sprites in Scratch are like digital puppets that we can control.
questions.explanation: The book explicitly compares sprites to digital puppets: you choose or create them and then control their movement and actions with blocks.

questions.question: Where can you get sprites for your Scratch project?
options: From the Scratch sprite library or by creating your own
questions.explanation: The book says you can choose sprites from a library or create your own -- there are two ways to get a sprite.

questions.question: Animation is like creating a moving picture story, similar to how cartoons are made.
questions.explanation: The chapter defines animation as 'like creating a moving picture story,' comparing it directly to how cartoons on television are made.

questions.question: Why does the book compare Scratch animation to cartoons on TV?
options: Because Scratch can only make cartoons, nothing else
Because in both cases we tell the characters exactly how to move, step by step, to create a moving story
Because cartoons and Scratch use the exact same software
Because both need a watering can sprite
questions.explanation: The book explains that when we create animation we 'tell the computer exactly how our characters should move, step by step' -- this step-by-step instruction-giving is exactly how cartoons are put together frame by frame.

questions.question: Which story do the crane and crab sprites come from in this chapter?
options: The Crafty Crane and the Clever Crab
questions.explanation: The chapter's animation project brings to life 'the story of the crafty crane and the clever crab' -- the two sprites needed are a crane sprite and a crab sprite.

questions.question: Which sprites are needed to tell the story used in this chapter's Scratch project? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: For 'The Crafty Crane and the Clever Crab' story you need a crane sprite and a crab sprite. The butterfly and watering can sprites belong to the later digital-plant-garden project, not this story.

questions.question: A picture in the book shows a boy pulling on a giant beanstalk growing up a castle wall. What classic story does this most likely remind you of?
options: The Crafty Crane and the Clever Crab
questions.explanation: The 'Get Set, Go!' picture of a boy named Jack with tall bean plants growing beside a castle wall is meant to remind readers of 'Jack and the Beanstalk' -- it is NOT the crane-and-crab story, which is a separate example used later for the Scratch animation.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT one of the block categories you can see in the Scratch block palette shown in the book (Motion, Looks, Sound, Events, Control, Sensing, Operators, Variables, My Blocks)?
questions.explanation: The Scratch screenshot in the book shows the categories Motion, Looks, Sound, Events, Control, Sensing, Operators, Variables and My Blocks. 'Fractions' is a chapter topic, not a Scratch block category.

questions.question: The Scratch interface shown in the book has a 'Variables' category in its block palette.
questions.explanation: The left-hand palette in the Scratch screenshot lists categories including Variables (along with Motion, Looks, Sound, Events, Control, Sensing, Operators and My Blocks), which is where blocks like 'water level' and 'growth stage' come from.

questions.question: What does the chapter title 'The Learning Web' introduce students to?
options: Using Scratch to animate stories, show fractions, and simulate a growing digital plant
questions.explanation: The chapter's three sub-topics are Animation and Storytelling with Scratch, Fractions Come Alive with Technology, and Growing Digital Plants with Scratch -- all built using the Scratch programming tool.

questions.question: How many growth-stage costumes are shown for the digital plant in the book (seed, sprout, young plant, mature plant)?
questions.explanation: The book shows exactly 4 costume pictures labelled 'Costumes for the 4 stages of the plant': seed, sprout, young plant, and mature plant.

questions.question: A student says, 'Scratch is only useful for making animations, it can't help with fractions or plants.' What is wrong with this statement?
options: It is wrong -- this chapter uses Scratch for THREE different things: animation, fractions with the pen tool, and a digital plant simulation
Scratch can only be used for plants, not animation
questions.explanation: The chapter shows Scratch is a flexible tool: it is used for animating a story (crane and crab), for drawing fraction shapes with the pen tool, and for simulating a growing digital plant with variables -- three very different uses of the same program.

questions.question: In Scratch, you must always draw your own sprites -- you are not allowed to choose one from a library.
questions.explanation: This is false. The book says you 'can choose sprites from a library or create your own,' so using the built-in library is allowed and often the easier option.

questions.question: The book says 'When we create animation, we tell the computer exactly how our characters should move, step by step.' What does this best describe?
options: A random, unplanned way of moving sprites
Sequencing -- giving the computer a precise, ordered set of instructions
questions.explanation: Telling the computer exactly how characters should move, step by step, is the essence of sequencing: the order of instructions matters and the computer follows them one after another.

questions.question: Which Scratch block makes a sprite walk forward a certain number of steps?
questions.explanation: The 'move steps' block is the basic movement block -- the book gives the example 'use the move steps block to walk characters forward.'

questions.question: What does the 'turn degrees' block do to a sprite?
options: Changes the direction it is facing
Sends a message to another sprite
questions.explanation: The turn degrees block changes the direction a character is facing -- it does not move the sprite forward, only rotates it.

questions.question: Which movement block instantly jumps a sprite to a location, without any walking animation in between?
questions.explanation: The 'go to' block moves characters instantly to a location -- the book notes this is 'useful for quick scene changes.'

questions.question: In the book review question about movement blocks, which block makes a character jump instantly to a location, and why is this different from 'glide'?
options: 'go to', because it teleports the sprite instantly with no smooth animation, unlike glide which moves smoothly over time
'turn degrees', because it rotates the sprite instantly
'move steps', because it always moves 100 steps at once
questions.explanation: 'go to' places a sprite at an exact position immediately (no animation), which is why it's good for 'quick scene changes,' while 'glide' (seen with the butterfly and crane) moves a sprite smoothly across the screen over a set number of seconds.

questions.question: Which block makes a character move smoothly, rather than jumping instantly?
questions.explanation: Glide blocks make characters move smoothly -- the book gives the example of using them 'for natural movements in animations,' like a crane flying over a lake.

questions.question: Which of these are true about the 'move steps' block? (Select all that apply)
options: It can only make big movements, never small ones
You can adjust the step size to control how far/fast a character seems to move
A small number like 5 steps makes a small, slow-looking movement
It always moves a character to an exact x,y coordinate
questions.explanation: The 'move steps' block lets you set any step size -- small numbers (like 5) look like small/slow movements, bigger numbers (like 20) look like faster/bigger movements. It is FALSE that it can only make big steps, and moving to an exact x,y coordinate is what 'go to' does, not 'move steps'.

questions.question: The 'move steps' block can only make characters take big steps, never small ones.
questions.explanation: This is false -- the MILESTONE review explicitly marks this statement False, since you can set the move steps block to any number, including small ones for slow, careful movement.

questions.question: A student wants their crane sprite to fly back and forth between two lakes many times using the fewest blocks possible. Which single block should hold the flying movement blocks inside it?
options: A single 'move steps' block used once
questions.explanation: Repeating flying movements many times is exactly what a loop is for -- putting the movement blocks inside a 'repeat' block (e.g. 'repeat 5') makes the crane fly back and forth automatically without duplicating blocks.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the 'point in direction' setting seen with the watering can and crane sprites?
options: To set which way the sprite is facing on the stage
questions.explanation: 'point in direction 90' (as seen in the watering can and butterfly blocks) sets which way the sprite faces on the stage, which affects the direction it appears to move or look.

questions.question: In the crane-and-crab story, movement blocks were used to make characters 'look at each other.' Which block is most directly responsible for this?
questions.explanation: The 'turn degrees' block changes the direction a character faces, which the book directly connects to making characters 'look at each other in your animations.'

questions.question: According to the book, connecting movement blocks together in order creates what?
options: A complete movement sequence that the computer follows one instruction at a time
questions.explanation: The book states: 'When we connect these blocks together, we create a complete movement sequence. The computer will follow our instructions one by one.'

questions.question: The 'go to' block and the 'glide' block do exactly the same thing on the stage.
questions.explanation: They do not do the same thing: 'go to' instantly teleports a sprite to a position (no animation), while 'glide' smoothly animates the sprite moving to that position over time -- useful for natural-looking movement like a flying crane.

questions.question: What is 'sequencing' in Scratch, according to the book?
options: Organizing actions in order, like reading a story from beginning to end
questions.explanation: The book compares sequencing in Scratch to 'reading a story from beginning to end' -- it means putting movement blocks in the correct order so the computer performs them in that exact sequence.

questions.question: Why does the order of blocks matter when programming a character's actions?
options: It doesn't matter -- Scratch runs blocks in any order it likes
The computer follows instructions one by one in the order given, so a wrong order gives the wrong result
Only the last block in a stack actually runs
Order only matters for fractions, not animation
questions.explanation: Because Scratch executes a stack of blocks one instruction at a time from top to bottom, changing the order changes what actually happens on screen -- e.g. turning before moving gives a different result than moving before turning.

questions.question: In the crane-and-crab animation, a sequence might be: 'move 50 steps, turn 180 degrees, say I am hungry for 2 seconds.' What is this an example of?
options: Sequencing -- a series of blocks run in a planned order
questions.explanation: This ordered list of blocks -- move, then turn, then say -- is a sequence: each instruction happens after the previous one finishes, in the order they were placed.

questions.question: A student swaps the order of 'turn 180 degrees' and 'move 50 steps' in their crab's sequence. What is the most likely result?
options: The crab moves in a different direction than intended, because turning before moving changes which way it walks
Scratch will show an error and refuse to run
The crab will say 'I am hungry' automatically
questions.explanation: Since the crab moves in whatever direction it is currently facing, turning before moving (instead of after) changes the direction of the move -- this shows why the exact order of steps in a sequence matters.

questions.question: Sequencing means putting instructions in a planned order so a character performs actions correctly, one after another.
questions.explanation: This matches the book's definition: sequencing in Scratch is like reading a story from beginning to end -- actions happen in the order you place the blocks.

questions.question: Which crossword answer describes 'putting movement blocks in the right order, like reading a story from beginning to end'?
questions.explanation: The book's own review crossword clue for 'Sequencing' is exactly this description: putting movement blocks in the right order, like reading a story from beginning to end.

questions.question: How is sequencing different from coordination in this chapter?
options: They are exactly the same thing
Sequencing is about the ORDER of one sprite's own blocks; coordination is about making MULTIPLE sprites work together correctly using messages
Coordination only applies to the crane sprite
questions.explanation: Sequencing is about a single sprite following its own instructions in the right order, while coordination (using broadcast/receive) is about making sure two or more sprites interact and respond to each other at the right time.

questions.question: What do loops in Scratch do?
options: Repeat actions automatically, saving time by avoiding repetitive coding
questions.explanation: The book states: 'Loops in Scratch repeat actions automatically... They save time by avoiding repetitive coding.'

questions.question: Which block repeats the actions inside it a specific, fixed number of times?
questions.explanation: The 'repeat' block loops actions a certain number of times -- e.g. 'repeat 10' runs the blocks inside it exactly 10 times.

questions.question: In the worksheet, what does the orange 'repeat 10' block do?
options: Repeats the actions inside it 10 times
questions.explanation: The worksheet's tick-the-correct-option question confirms the 'repeat 10' block repeats whatever actions are placed inside it exactly 10 times.

questions.question: The 'repeat' block helps us do the same action multiple times automatically.
questions.explanation: This True/False worksheet item is answered True: the repeat block is designed specifically to run the same set of actions multiple times without you re-adding the blocks.

questions.question: The 'forever' block runs commands exactly 10 times and then stops.
questions.explanation: This is False. The correct statement (from the worksheet's own correction) is: 'The forever block runs commands continuously without stopping' -- it never stops on its own, unlike 'repeat 10' which stops after 10 times.

questions.question: What is the key difference between the 'repeat' block and the 'forever' block?
options: There is no difference, they behave identically
'repeat' runs a set number of times and then stops; 'forever' runs continuously and never stops on its own
'forever' only works with the crab sprite
'repeat' can never be used with movement blocks
questions.explanation: 'repeat' (e.g. 'repeat 10') performs its actions a fixed number of times and then stops, while 'forever' loops its actions endlessly -- useful for background actions like water moving or fish swimming continuously.

questions.question: According to the book, what is the 'forever' block especially useful for?
options: Background actions that should never stop, like making lake water move constantly
questions.explanation: The book says the forever block 'creates a loop that never stops. This is useful for background actions, like making water in the lake move constantly or having fish swim around continuously.'

questions.question: Which of these statements about loops are TRUE? (Select all that apply)
options: 'repeat 5' would make a crane fly back and forth between two lakes exactly 5 times
The forever block is ideal for continuous background motion
Loops save time by avoiding writing the same blocks again and again
questions.explanation: 'repeat 5' does run its actions 5 times, forever loops suit constant background motion, and loops in general save time by avoiding repeated blocks. It is FALSE that 'forever' stops after 10 repeats -- that describes 'repeat 10', not 'forever'.

questions.question: What does a 'repeat until growth stage = 4' block do in the digital plant project?
options: Keeps repeating the blocks inside it until the plant's growth stage variable becomes 4, then stops
questions.explanation: 'repeat until' is a loop that keeps running until its condition becomes true. Here it keeps checking the plant's care conditions until growth stage reaches 4 (fully mature), then the loop stops.

questions.question: In the digital plant project, the three 'if...then' checks for seed-to-sprout, sprout-to-young, and young-to-mature growth are placed inside which loop block?
questions.explanation: The book shows: 'repeat loop till growth stage 4: the 3 if...then loops go inside the repeat loop' -- meaning the growth-stage checks are nested inside a 'repeat until growth stage = 4' loop.

questions.question: Because 'forever' loops never stop by themselves, they should never be used anywhere in a Scratch project.
questions.explanation: This is false. 'Forever' loops ARE useful and are recommended by the book for things that should run continuously in the background, like water moving or fish swimming -- the key is to use them for the RIGHT purpose, not to avoid them entirely.

questions.question: A student wants water in a lake background to keep moving the entire time the animation plays, with no set number of repeats. Which loop block fits best?
questions.explanation: Because there's no fixed number of repeats needed -- the water should move for as long as the program runs -- the 'forever' block is the right choice, exactly as the book describes for continuous background motion.

questions.question: If you want a character to repeat an action a certain number of times, which block would you use to hold those actions?
questions.explanation: The repeat block is used to loop actions a certain number of times, as opposed to 'forever' which loops without any set limit.

questions.question: Which two blocks work together to send and receive messages between sprites in Scratch?
questions.explanation: The worksheet's fill-in-the-blank confirms: when we want two sprites to work together, we use 'broadcast' and 'when I receive' blocks to send messages between them.

questions.question: What does coordination mean in the context of this chapter's Scratch project?
options: Allowing multiple characters to interact correctly with each other
questions.explanation: The book defines coordination as what 'allows multiple characters to interact correctly,' achieved using broadcast blocks to send messages between characters.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the 'broadcast' block?
options: To send messages to start actions in other sprites
To change the backdrop colour only
questions.explanation: The broadcast block sends messages to start actions -- the book gives the example of coordinating multiple sprites in an animation this way.

questions.question: The 'broadcast' and 'when I receive' blocks help characters work together by sending messages that all characters can hear.
questions.explanation: This matches the book's MILESTONE review answer: broadcast messages are heard by all sprites listening for that message, which is how sprites coordinate their actions with one another.

questions.question: In the digital plant project, what happens when the plant becomes mature?
options: The plant broadcasts a 'plant mature' message, which the butterfly sprite listens for so it knows to appear
questions.explanation: The plant's mature-stage blocks include 'broadcast plant mature and wait' -- the butterfly sprite is programmed to receive this exact message and show itself when it hears it.

questions.question: In the crane-and-crab example, what real thing does the 'broadcast' block let a crane sprite do?
options: Move instantly to a new location
Send a message, like making a crane say 'I'm hungry!' as part of a coordinated sequence
Erase the drawing on the pen tool
questions.explanation: The book's programming example uses a series of blocks -- including broadcast -- to make a crane say 'I'm hungry!' as part of coordinating the animated story between the crane and crab.

questions.question: Which of the following use the broadcast/receive message system in this chapter? (Select all that apply)
options: The watering can sprite broadcasting 'water plant' when clicked
The plant broadcasting 'plant mature' so the butterfly appears
The 'move steps' block moving a sprite forward
The 'S' key press changing sunlight hours directly (not via broadcast)
questions.explanation: Both the watering can ('broadcast water plant' when clicked) and the mature plant ('broadcast plant mature') use messages to coordinate with other sprites. 'move steps' is a plain motion block, and the 'S' key press changes the sunlight hours variable directly using a 'when key pressed' + 'change variable' block, without any broadcast.

questions.question: Why can't the plant sprite just tell the butterfly sprite directly to 'become visible' using the plant's own blocks?
options: It actually can, and that's exactly what happens
In Scratch, one sprite's blocks can't directly control another sprite's costume/visibility -- sprites must communicate using broadcast/receive messages instead
Because only the watering can sprite can broadcast messages
questions.explanation: In Scratch, each sprite has its own independent set of blocks; a sprite cannot reach into another sprite's scripts directly. That's exactly why 'broadcast' and 'when I receive' exist -- they let one sprite (the plant) signal an event that another sprite (the butterfly) can react to on its own.

questions.question: What does 'coordination' let multiple Scratch characters do?
options: Interact correctly with each other, for example through broadcast messages
questions.explanation: Coordination allows multiple characters to interact correctly -- the book's example is using broadcast blocks to send messages between characters so their actions line up properly.

questions.question: Which crossword answer means 'making sure characters do the right things at the right time when working together'?
questions.explanation: The book's own crossword clue defines coordination exactly this way: making sure characters do the right things at the right time when working together.

questions.question: What does a 'backdrop' set in a Scratch project?
options: The colour of a sprite's costume
The background of your Scratch story
questions.explanation: The backdrop sets the background scene of your Scratch story -- the book notes you can customize scenes with different backdrops.

questions.question: Why does the book say adding multiple characters makes a story more interesting?
options: It allows for interactions between characters in the story
It removes the need for a backdrop
questions.explanation: The book states that 'adding multiple characters makes stories more interesting' because it creates real-life-style interactions between the characters, like the crane and the crab.

questions.question: According to the book, when adding multiple characters to a scene, what must be done for each one?
options: Each character needs its own set of movement blocks, and their actions must be timed carefully so they interact properly
Only one character can have blocks at a time
All characters must share exactly the same blocks
questions.explanation: The book explains: 'Each character needs its own set of movement blocks. We can make them interact with each other by timing their actions carefully' -- so both the crane and crab need separate scripts that are coordinated in time.

questions.question: You can customize a Scratch scene by choosing different backdrops.
questions.explanation: The book explicitly says to 'customize scenes with different backdrops,' confirming that changing the backdrop is a normal part of building a Scratch story scene.

questions.question: A student adds a crab sprite to their project but never gives it any of its own movement blocks. What will most likely happen?
options: The crab will automatically copy the crane's blocks
The crab sprite will not move or act on its own, since each character needs its own separate set of blocks
The crab will turn into a butterfly
questions.explanation: Since 'each character needs its own set of movement blocks,' a sprite with no blocks attached simply will not do anything by itself -- blocks are not automatically shared between sprites.

questions.question: In the crane-and-crab animation shown in the book, where are the two characters standing?
options: On a beach near the water, with the crane on the sand and the crab nearby
On top of a bean plant
questions.explanation: The Scratch stage screenshot shows a beach scene with the sea in the background, the crane standing on the sand, and the crab sprite next to it.

questions.question: What do fractions represent?
questions.explanation: The book states plainly: 'Fractions represent parts of a whole' -- for example, eating half a pizza is like consuming 1/2 of it.

questions.question: Which Scratch tool helps you draw shapes to show fractions, like a digital crayon on the screen?
questions.explanation: The pen tool in Scratch helps draw shapes -- the book compares it to 'using a digital crayon on screen.'

questions.question: What do 'division lines' do when drawing a fraction shape in Scratch?
options: They create equal parts within a shape
questions.explanation: Drawing division lines creates equal parts in shapes -- for example, dividing a square into 4 equal parts to show fractions.

questions.question: What is one way Scratch helps make fraction parts visually clear?
options: By colouring different parts with the pen tool's colour setting
By turning the shape into a sprite
questions.explanation: Colouring parts in Scratch illustrates fractions visually -- changing pen colours lets you represent different fraction parts, like colouring some slices of a circle differently from others.

questions.question: Which shape does the book use as an example for showing fractions like pizza slices?
questions.explanation: The book states that circles can be divided to show fractions like pizza slices, giving the real-life application of creating circle fractions to make learning fun.

questions.question: In Scratch, what block combination is used to draw a square divided into 4 equal parts using the pen tool?
questions.explanation: The book's pen-tool example draws a square by repeating 4 times: move 100 steps, then turn 90 degrees -- since a square has 4 equal sides and 4 right-angle turns.

questions.question: Before drawing a new pen shape in Scratch, what steps does the book show being used to prepare the canvas?
options: Erase all, then set the pen colour and pen size, then pen down
questions.explanation: The pen tool steps shown are: erase all (clear old drawings), pen up, set pen colour, set pen size, then pen down -- preparing a clean canvas with the right colour/size before drawing.

questions.question: What does the fraction 1/2 represent, using the book's pizza example?
questions.explanation: The book gives the example: 'Eating half a pizza is like consuming 1/2 of it' -- 1/2 means one part out of two equal parts.

questions.question: What does the fraction 3/4 represent when a square is divided into 4 equal parts and 3 of them are coloured?
options: One quarter of the square is coloured
Three quarters of the square is coloured
None of the square is coloured
questions.explanation: If a square is split into 4 equal parts and 3 of those parts are coloured, that represents the fraction 3/4 -- three parts out of four equal parts.

questions.question: A fraction like 2/3 means we have 2 parts out of 3 equal parts of something.
questions.explanation: This matches the worksheet's answer key: 2/3 correctly means 2 parts out of 3 equal parts of a whole.

questions.question: When we colour 3 parts red in a square divided into 4 equal parts, we show the fraction 3/4.
questions.explanation: This is confirmed True in the book's review: colouring 3 out of 4 equal parts represents the fraction 3/4, since fractions describe a number of equal parts out of the total number of equal parts.

questions.question: A student divides a circle into 4 unequal slices (one huge, three tiny) and colours one of the tiny slices. Can they correctly call this '1/4' of the circle?
options: Yes, any coloured slice out of 4 slices is always 1/4
No -- fractions require the parts to be EQUAL; unequal slices cannot be labelled as simple fractions like 1/4
Yes, because circles are always divided fairly
No, because circles cannot show fractions at all
questions.explanation: Fractions describe equal parts of a whole. The book's fraction examples (square into 4 equal parts, circle sliced like a pizza) all rely on the parts being the same size -- unequal slices break the basic idea of a fraction like 1/4.

questions.question: Which of these are TRUE about using the pen tool to show fractions in Scratch? (Select all that apply)
options: Division lines create equal parts within a shape
Changing pen colour can represent different fraction parts
The pen tool can only draw circles, never squares
Fractions represent parts of a whole
questions.explanation: Division lines make equal parts, colouring shows different fraction parts, and fractions represent parts of a whole -- all true per the book. It is FALSE that the pen tool can only draw circles; the book explicitly shows drawing squares (repeat 4, move 100, turn 90) as well as circles.

questions.question: Why might Scratch's pen tool be described as being 'like using a digital crayon on screen'?
options: Because it lets you draw lines and shapes directly on the stage, just like colouring with a crayon on paper
Because it only works with fractions
questions.explanation: The comparison to a digital crayon captures how the pen tool lets a sprite draw lines/shapes as it moves across the stage, similar to how a crayon draws marks as you move it across paper.

questions.question: What are 'variables' in Scratch used for, according to the book?
options: They store important information, like memory boxes for your program
They change the backdrop colour permanently
They are another name for sprites
questions.explanation: The book describes variables as things that 'store important information like water levels... They act like memory boxes for your program.'

questions.question: Which THREE variables are used to track the digital plant's condition in this chapter's simulation? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: The digital plant simulation tracks three variables shown on the Scratch stage: Water level, Sunlight hours, and Plant age. There is no 'crossword score' variable in this project.

questions.question: How many growth stages does a digital plant have in this simulation?
questions.explanation: The worksheet fill-in-the-blank confirms: 'A digital plant has four growth stages: seed, sprout, young plant, and mature plant.'

questions.question: What is the correct order of the digital plant's growth stages?
questions.explanation: The correct order of plant growth stages, confirmed in the book, is seed, sprout, young plant, then mature -- each stage requires specific care before moving to the next.

questions.question: The correct order of plant growth stages is seed, sprout, young plant, mature.
questions.explanation: This directly matches the book's fact: 'The correct order of plant growth stages is seed, sprout, young plant, mature. Each stage requires specific care.'

questions.question: How much water and sunlight does the digital plant need to grow from 'seed' to 'sprout'?
options: 20 units of water and 10 hours of sunlight
questions.explanation: According to the book's growth-stage diagram, a digital plant needs 20 units of water and 10 hours of sunlight to move from the seed stage to the sprout stage.

questions.question: How much water and sunlight does the digital plant need to grow from 'sprout' to 'young plant'?
options: 40 units of water and 20 hours of sunlight
questions.explanation: The book's growth diagram shows the sprout-to-young-plant transition requires 40 units of water and 20 hours of sunlight -- double the requirement of the seed-to-sprout stage.

questions.question: How much water and sunlight does the digital plant need to grow from 'young plant' to 'mature'?
options: 60 units of water and 30 hours of sunlight
questions.explanation: The final growth stage requires the most care: 60 units of water and 30 hours of sunlight to move from young plant to mature, continuing the pattern of increasing requirements at each stage.

questions.question: Looking at the pattern 20/10, 40/20, 60/30 for water/sunlight needed at each growth stage, what do you notice?
options: The numbers decrease at each stage
Both water and sunlight requirements increase by the same amount (20 water, 10 sunlight) at each stage, and water is always double the sunlight hours
The numbers are random with no pattern
Sunlight requirements are always higher than water requirements
questions.explanation: Each stage adds exactly 20 more units of water and 10 more hours of sunlight than the previous stage (20/10, then 40/20, then 60/30), and at every stage the water number is exactly double the sunlight number.

questions.question: In our digital plant simulation, the plant grows to the next stage only when it has enough water and what else?
questions.explanation: The worksheet fill-in-the-blank confirms: 'the plant will grow to the next stage only when it has enough water and sunlight.'

questions.question: Which block type checks a condition (like water level > 60 AND sunlight hours > 30) before letting the plant move to the next growth stage?
questions.explanation: The book shows nested 'if...then' blocks that check conditions like 'water level > 60 and sunlight hours > 30' combined with 'growth stage = 3' before switching the plant to its mature costume.

questions.question: What does the 'growth stage' variable represent in the digital plant project?
options: A number tracking which of the 4 growth stages the plant is currently in
questions.explanation: 'Growth stage' is a variable used to track which stage (out of the 4: seed, sprout, young plant, mature) the digital plant currently is in -- for example, growth stage = 3 means young plant, and growth stage = 4 means mature.

questions.question: How does the digital plant know when to grow to the next stage?
options: It grows automatically after a fixed amount of time passes
It checks if it has received enough water and sunlight
It grows when we click on it with the mouse
It grows when we change its costume or appearance
questions.explanation: This exact question appears on the worksheet, and the correct tick is: the plant checks if it has received enough water and sunlight -- growth is condition-based, not simply time-based or click-based.

questions.question: To create realistic plant growth, you should make all growth stages happen instantly without checking water and sunlight levels.
questions.explanation: This is False, per the worksheet's own correction: 'Realistic plant growth should check water and sunlight levels before advancing to the next stage' -- growth should be earned through proper care, not instant.

questions.question: What is a good way to describe what a 'variable' does in a program, using the book's own comparison?
options: It acts like a memory box that stores information your program needs to remember
It is another word for a sprite costume
It only works with the pen tool
questions.explanation: The book directly compares variables to 'memory boxes for your program' -- they store values (like water level) that the program can check and update over time.

questions.question: Which of these are needed for a plant to move from 'young plant' (growth stage 3) to 'mature' (growth stage 4) in this simulation? (Select all that apply)
options: A butterfly must already be visible
questions.explanation: The mature-stage check requires water level > 60 AND sunlight hours > 30 AND growth stage = 3 (meaning it's currently a young plant) before switching to mature. The butterfly's visibility is not a requirement for the plant to mature -- in fact the butterfly only appears AFTER the plant becomes mature.

questions.question: When setting up the digital plant at the very start, what values are variables like water level, sunlight hours, and plant age typically set to?
options: 0 (zero), since the plant is just starting as a seed
questions.explanation: At the start of the simulation the plant is a fresh seed, so water level, sunlight hours, and plant age are all set to 0, and growth stage is set to 1 (seed).

questions.question: Why does the plant need an 'if...then' check for EACH growth stage (seed-to-sprout, sprout-to-young, young-to-mature) instead of just one big check for the whole simulation?
options: Because each stage transition needs its own water/sunlight threshold and must only apply when the plant is actually at that specific starting stage
Because Scratch does not allow more than one if-then block
Because each check controls a different backdrop colour
There is no real reason, it is just decoration
questions.explanation: Each stage has a different water/sunlight requirement (20/10, 40/20, 60/30) and should only trigger when the plant is currently AT that stage (checked via the growth stage variable) -- so three separate if-then checks are needed, one per transition, all inside the repeat-until loop.

questions.question: What happens to a digital plant when it doesn't get enough water?
questions.explanation: The worksheet's tick-the-correct-option confirms: when a digital plant doesn't get enough water, it becomes wilted.

questions.question: If a digital plant is wilting because of too little water, which sprite should you click to increase the water level?
questions.explanation: The worksheet fill-in-the-blank confirms: if your digital plant is wilting because of too little water, click on the watering can sprite to increase the water level variable.

questions.question: At what water level does the digital plant start wilting and looking brown and droopy?
questions.explanation: The book states: 'Wilting happens when our plant doesn't get enough water. If the water level goes below 5 over time, our plant will look brown and droopy' and say 'I'm wilting! Need water!'

questions.question: At what water level does the digital plant become overwatered and look yellow and sick?
questions.explanation: The book states: 'Overwatering happens when we give too much water. If the water level goes above 100, our plant will look yellow and sick' and say 'Too much water! I'm drowning!'

questions.question: What can overwatering do to a digital plant, according to the book?
options: Make it look yellow and sick
Make it turn into a butterfly
questions.explanation: Overwatering can make plants look yellow and sick -- the book advises balancing water levels to keep digital plants healthy.

questions.question: A plant's water level is exactly 3. What is most likely to happen to the plant?
options: It will grow to the mature stage instantly
It will start wilting and look brown/droopy, since 3 is below the wilting threshold of 5
It will become overwatered and yellow
questions.explanation: Since the wilting condition triggers when water level goes below 5, a water level of 3 falls below that threshold, so the plant will start wilting, looking brown and droopy, and saying 'I'm wilting! Need water!'

questions.question: A plant's water level is 150. What is most likely to happen?
options: It will wilt from lack of water
It will become overwatered and look yellow and sick, since 150 is above the overwatering threshold of 100
It will stay perfectly healthy no matter what
It will immediately become a butterfly
questions.explanation: Since overwatering triggers when the water level goes above 100, a level of 150 is well past that threshold -- the plant will look yellow and sick and say 'Too much water! I'm drowning!'

questions.question: Which sprite adds water to the digital plant when clicked?
questions.explanation: Clicking the watering can sprite broadcasts a 'water plant' message and is how the player waters the digital plant in the simulation.

questions.question: How does a player add sunlight hours to the digital plant, based on the book's example blocks?
options: By clicking the watering can sprite
By pressing the 'S' key, which changes the sunlight hours variable by 10 and shows the message 'Sunshine feels great!'
By clicking on the crossword puzzle
questions.explanation: The book shows a 'when S key pressed' block that changes the sunlight hours variable by 10 and makes the plant say 'Sunshine feels great!' for 1 second -- this is how sunlight is added in the simulation.

questions.question: Balance in care -- not giving too much or too little water/sunlight -- is necessary for the digital plant's health.
questions.explanation: The book states: 'Balance in care is necessary for plant health... Too much or too little water affects growth,' matching both the wilting (too little) and overwatering (too much) problems.

questions.question: Which of these are real plant 'problems' described in the book's digital plant simulation? (Select all that apply)
options: The plant turning into a crab
The plant looking yellow and sick
questions.explanation: The two real problems described are wilting (too little water, water level below 5) and overwatering (too much water, water level above 100, causing a yellow/sick look). The plant does not turn into a crab -- that is not part of this simulation at all.

questions.question: What does the digital plant say when it is overwatered?
questions.explanation: When overwatered (water level above 100) the book's plant sprite says 'Too much water! I'm drowning!' to signal it has received too much water.

questions.question: What does the digital plant say when it becomes fully mature?
questions.explanation: When the plant reaches the mature stage, it switches costume, sets growth stage to 4, and says 'I'm fully grown!' for 2 seconds before broadcasting 'plant mature'.

questions.question: Taking care of a digital plant, according to the book, involves adding what two things?
questions.explanation: The book states: 'Taking care of digital plants involves adding water and sunlight,' simulated in Scratch using simple commands.

questions.question: A mature digital plant needs unlimited amounts of water to stay healthy.
questions.explanation: This is false, per the book's MILESTONE review: a mature plant does NOT need unlimited water -- too much water (above 100) causes overwatering and makes the plant look yellow and sick. Balance is always required.

questions.question: When does a butterfly visit the digital garden, according to the book?
options: As soon as the seed is planted
When plants mature and have flowers
Only when the crossword is solved
questions.explanation: Adding butterflies makes digital gardens lively -- the book's real-life application is that 'butterflies visit when plants mature and have flowers.'

questions.question: What special flying pattern do butterflies have in this chapter's Scratch animations?
options: They change costumes to look like they are flapping their wings
questions.explanation: The book's fun fact says butterflies 'change costumes to look like they are flapping wings' -- this costume-switching creates the illusion of a flying motion.

questions.question: How does the butterfly sprite know when to appear on screen?
options: It appears immediately when the program starts
It receives the 'plant mature' broadcast message from the plant sprite and then shows itself
It appears when the watering can is clicked
It appears when the pen tool is used
questions.explanation: The book explains: 'When the butterfly receives the message that our plant is mature, it will appear on the screen. It will show itself and start flying around' -- so it depends on the broadcast message from the plant.

questions.question: Which behaviours does the butterfly have, according to the book's Step 5/6 description? (Select all that apply)
options: Stay hidden when the plant is young
Appear when the plant grows flowers
questions.explanation: The book lists the butterfly's behaviours as: stay hidden when young, appear when flowers grow, fly around the mature plant, and change costume to look like flying. Watering the plant is the watering can sprite's job, not the butterfly's.

questions.question: What does communication between the plant and the butterfly use, according to the book?
questions.explanation: The book states: 'Communication between plants and butterflies uses messages... A mature plant sends a message to invite a butterfly.'

questions.question: Interactivity -- like the butterfly reacting to plant growth -- makes the garden simulation more engaging.
questions.explanation: The book states that 'Interactivity makes the garden simulation engaging,' referring to features like the butterfly reacting to messages sent by the plant.

questions.question: What does taking care of a digital garden teach, according to the book?
options: Responsibility -- since regular care helps plants grow healthy and attracts butterflies
questions.explanation: The book states: 'Digital gardens teach responsibility in plant care. Regular care helps plants grow healthy and attracts butterflies.'

questions.question: Which crossword answer means 'garden creature that appears when plants grow flowers and makes the garden feel alive'?
questions.explanation: The book's own review crossword defines this clue as 'Butterfly' -- confirming the butterfly's role as the creature that appears once the plant has flowered.

questions.question: If a student's digital plant never reaches the mature stage (e.g. it keeps wilting from too little water), what will most likely happen to the butterfly?
options: It will appear anyway, regardless of the plant's stage
It will stay hidden, since it only appears after receiving the 'plant mature' broadcast message
It will turn into a crab
It will water the plant for the student
questions.explanation: Since the butterfly only shows itself after receiving the 'plant mature' broadcast message, a plant that never matures (because it keeps wilting) will never trigger that message, so the butterfly will stay hidden.

questions.question: What real-life idea does adding butterflies to the digital garden connect to?
options: Butterflies visiting flowering plants in real gardens
Watering cans in real life have no connection
questions.explanation: The digital butterfly mimics a real-life idea: butterflies are attracted to and visit gardens once plants flower, which the Scratch project recreates through the 'plant mature' message.

questions.question: In the book's review crossword, which word answers the clue 'moving pictures that tell a story'?
questions.explanation: The crossword answer for 'moving pictures that tell a story' is ANIMATION, matching the chapter's very first sub-topic.

questions.question: In the book's review crossword, which word answers the clue 'combining programming with math concepts'?
questions.explanation: The crossword answer is INTEGRATION -- referring to how this chapter combines programming (Scratch) with a math concept (fractions).

questions.question: In the book's review crossword, which word answers the clue 'parts of a whole number or object'?
questions.explanation: The crossword answer is FRACTIONS -- 'parts of a whole number or object' is the exact definition used throughout the chapter.

questions.question: In the book's review crossword, which word answers the clue 'the smooth change from one stage to another'?
questions.explanation: The crossword answer is TRANSITION -- describing the smooth change between growth stages or scenes, such as the plant moving from one growth stage to the next.

questions.question: In the book's review crossword, which word answers the clue 'doing the same action multiple times automatically'?
questions.explanation: The crossword answer is LOOP -- exactly matching the chapter's definition of loops as blocks (repeat/forever) that repeat actions automatically.

questions.question: In the earlier worksheet crossword puzzle, which word fills in for 'sprites'-related characters (digital puppets) in Scratch?
questions.explanation: Sprites are the digital puppet-like characters in Scratch -- this vocabulary word appears throughout both the worksheet fill-in-the-blanks and the crossword puzzles in this chapter.

questions.question: The book's second review crossword includes the clue 'memory boxes that help us remember important info like water level and plant age.' Which vocabulary word is this?
questions.explanation: This clue describes VARIABLES -- the book repeatedly compares variables to 'memory boxes' that store information such as water level, sunlight hours, plant age, and growth stage.

questions.question: Which of these words are answers to clues in the book's SECOND review crossword puzzle (page 54)? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: The second crossword's answers are SPRITES (digital characters/puppets), BUTTERFLY (garden creature appearing at maturity), and VARIABLES (memory boxes for water level/plant age). FRACTIONS was an answer in the FIRST review crossword (page 54, top set), which is a different puzzle in the worksheet materials -- keep the two crosswords' clue sets distinct.

questions.question: Which vocabulary word from this chapter means 'digital characters in Scratch that act like puppets we can control'?
questions.explanation: This is the crossword's own definition for SPRITES -- digital characters in Scratch that act like puppets we can control.

questions.question: This chapter, 'The Learning Web,' is built around which THREE main Scratch-based activities?
options: Animating a story, showing fractions with the pen tool, and growing a digital plant
questions.explanation: The chapter's sub-topics are: Animation and Storytelling with Scratch, Fractions Come Alive with Technology, and Growing Digital Plants with Scratch -- three connected Scratch projects.

questions.question: Which of the following are Scratch block types mentioned across this chapter? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: move steps, repeat, and broadcast are all real Scratch blocks used throughout the chapter's projects. 'Crossword' is a paper-based review activity, not a Scratch block.

questions.question: How are 'sequencing' and 'loops' related but different in this chapter?
options: Sequencing is about the ORDER of individual instructions; loops let you REPEAT a sequence of instructions automatically instead of writing them again and again
Loops always run in reverse order
questions.explanation: Sequencing is about arranging instructions in the correct order (like a story), while loops (repeat/forever/repeat until) let you take a sequence and run it multiple times automatically, saving the effort of duplicating blocks.

questions.question: What variable tracks how many growth stages a digital plant has completed?
questions.explanation: 'Growth stage' is the variable that tracks which of the 4 stages (seed=1, sprout=2, young plant=3, mature=4) the plant is currently in.

questions.question: A student says: 'Water level, sunlight hours, plant age, and growth stage are all just decorations -- they don't actually control anything in the simulation.' Is this correct?
options: No -- these variables directly control the plant's behaviour, such as when it wilts, becomes overwatered, or advances to the next growth stage
Only water level matters, the rest are decorations
Only growth stage matters, the rest are decorations
questions.explanation: These variables are functional, not decorative: water level and sunlight hours are checked by if-then conditions to decide wilting, overwatering, and stage advancement, and growth stage tracks and controls which costume/behaviour the plant currently has.

questions.question: Which of these pairs correctly match a Scratch concept with its purpose in this chapter? (Select all that apply)
options: Broadcast/receive -> coordinating sprites like the plant and butterfly
Backdrop -> storing water level as a number
questions.explanation: Pen tool is correctly used for drawing fraction shapes, broadcast/receive for coordinating sprites, and repeat/forever for looping. It is FALSE that 'backdrop' stores water level as a number -- that is the job of a VARIABLE, not a backdrop.

questions.question: When making an interactive story, what can you use to trigger different character actions and responses?
questions.explanation: This True/False review item confirms: when making an interactive story, you can use keyboard keys (like the 'S' key for sunlight) to trigger different character actions and responses.

questions.question: When making an interactive story, you can use keyboard keys to trigger different character actions and responses.
questions.explanation: This is confirmed True by the worksheet's answer key -- keyboard key presses (like 'when S key pressed' for adding sunlight) are one way to trigger actions in an interactive Scratch story.

questions.question: Which growth-stage requirement pairs correctly match water level to sunlight hours needed for that transition?
options: Seed->Sprout: 20 water/10 sunlight; Sprout->Young: 40 water/20 sunlight; Young->Mature: 60 water/30 sunlight
Seed->Sprout: 60 water/30 sunlight; Sprout->Young: 40 water/20 sunlight; Young->Mature: 20 water/10 sunlight
All stages require exactly 50 water and 25 sunlight
Water and sunlight requirements are never specified
questions.explanation: The correct increasing pattern (confirmed from the book's growth-stage diagram) is: Seed->Sprout needs 20 water/10 sunlight, Sprout->Young needs 40 water/20 sunlight, and Young->Mature needs 60 water/30 sunlight.

questions.question: Considering both the wilting rule (water level below 5) and the overwatering rule (water level above 100), what water-level range keeps a digital plant safe from BOTH problems?
options: Between 5 and 100 (inclusive of values in between)
questions.explanation: Since wilting triggers below 5 and overwatering triggers above 100, a water level that stays between 5 and 100 avoids both problems -- illustrating the book's message that 'balance in care is necessary for plant health.'

questions.question: Which of these best summarizes the whole chapter, 'The Learning Web'?
options: A chapter only about watering real plants
A chapter that uses the Scratch programming tool to animate a story, visualize fractions, and simulate the care of a digital plant that attracts a butterfly
A chapter only about crossword puzzles
questions.explanation: The chapter ties together three connected Scratch activities -- animating the crane-and-crab story, drawing fraction shapes with the pen tool, and simulating a digital plant's growth and care (including a butterfly visitor) -- all under the theme of using Scratch as a learning tool.

questions.question: Which of these statements are TRUE about this chapter's overall content? (Select all that apply)
options: The crane and crab story uses movement, turn, and broadcast blocks together
The digital plant simulation uses variables and if-then/repeat-until blocks to manage growth
Fractions in this chapter are only shown using numbers, never pictures
The butterfly's appearance depends on a broadcast message from the plant, not a fixed timer
questions.explanation: The crane/crab story combines movement, turning, and broadcast blocks; the plant simulation relies on variables plus if-then/repeat-until logic; and the butterfly appears only after receiving the plant's 'plant mature' broadcast (not on a timer). It is FALSE that fractions are shown only using numbers -- the chapter repeatedly uses PICTURES (squares, circles, pizzas) coloured with the pen tool to show fractions visually.

questions.question: What is a 'costume' in Scratch?
options: A different look/appearance a sprite can switch to
questions.explanation: A costume is one of the different looks a sprite can have; switching costumes changes how a sprite appears, such as the watering can switching between 'watering can1' and 'watering can2' to look like it is pouring.

questions.question: In the watering can sprite's blocks, what happens after 'switch costume to watering can2'?
options: It waits 1 second, then switches to 'watering can1' again, animating a pouring action
It broadcasts a message to the crossword
questions.explanation: The watering can blocks show: switch costume to watering can2, wait 1 second, switch costume to watering can1 -- alternating between the two costumes creates the visual effect of the can pouring water.

questions.question: Why does the butterfly sprite change its costume repeatedly while flying?
options: To look like it is flapping its wings
To turn into a watering can
questions.explanation: The book's fun fact explains that butterflies 'change costumes to look like they are flapping wings' -- rapidly switching between wing-up and wing-down costumes creates a flying animation.

questions.question: Switching a sprite's costume can be used to create a simple animation effect, like a butterfly's flapping wings or a watering can pouring.
questions.explanation: This is exactly how the book's watering can and butterfly examples work: alternating between two costumes over time gives the illusion of pouring or flying.

questions.question: What do the coordinates 'x' and 'y' control for a sprite on the Scratch stage?
options: The sprite's exact position on the stage
The number of loops it runs
questions.explanation: x and y are coordinates that set a sprite's exact position on the stage -- seen for example in the watering can's blocks: 'go to x: -50 y: 0'.

questions.question: In the watering can sprite's 'when green flag clicked' script, what direction does it point in?
questions.explanation: The script shows 'go to x: -50 y: 0' followed by 'point in direction 90', which sets the sprite's starting position and facing direction when the green flag starts the project.

questions.question: Which event block starts a script as soon as the project begins running (the green flag is clicked)?
questions.explanation: 'when green flag clicked' is the event block that runs its attached script the moment you start the whole Scratch project, setting up starting positions like the watering can's.

questions.question: Which event block is used so that clicking directly on the watering can sprite makes it broadcast the 'water plant' message?
questions.explanation: The book shows 'when this sprite clicked' at the top of the watering can's script, followed by 'broadcast water plant' -- so clicking the sprite itself triggers the watering action.

questions.question: Clicking directly on the watering can sprite is what triggers it to broadcast the 'water plant' message.
questions.explanation: The watering can's script begins with 'when this sprite clicked', meaning the player must click the sprite itself (not press a key or click the green flag) to broadcast 'water plant'.

questions.question: A student presses the 'S' key to add sunlight but nothing happens, even though water is fine. What is the MOST likely cause?
options: The 'when S key pressed' script may be missing or the key press wasn't registered -- the sunlight hours variable only changes when this exact event block runs
Sunlight can only be added by clicking the watering can
The backdrop needs to change first
questions.explanation: Since sunlight is only added through the 'when S key pressed' event block (which changes sunlight hours by 10), if that script isn't present or the keypress isn't detected, sunlight simply won't increase -- there's no other way shown to add sunlight in this project.

questions.question: What does 'wait 1 seconds' do inside a costume-switching sequence?
options: Pauses the script for 1 second before the next block runs
questions.explanation: The 'wait 1 seconds' block simply pauses that sprite's script for 1 second, which is what gives costume-switching animations (like the watering can pouring) a visible, timed effect instead of happening instantly.

questions.question: In the crane story's beach scene, what is shown alongside the crane and crab sprites?
options: Sand, sea/water, and greenery as the backdrop
questions.explanation: The Scratch stage screenshot for the crane-and-crab animation shows a beach backdrop with sand, the sea, and greenery, with the crane and crab sprites placed on the sand.

questions.question: Which of the following are shown as part of the watering can sprite's full behaviour in the book? (Select all that apply)
options: Alternates between two costumes to look like pouring
Positions itself at a set x,y location when the green flag is clicked
Automatically waters the plant every 5 seconds without being clicked
questions.explanation: The watering can broadcasts 'water plant' when clicked, alternates its two costumes to animate pouring, and sets its starting x,y position on green flag. It is FALSE that it waters automatically every 5 seconds -- watering only happens when the player clicks the sprite.

questions.question: What visual technique makes a static picture look like it is 'flying' or 'pouring' in Scratch?
options: Quickly alternating between two or more costumes over short waits
Deleting the sprite and recreating it
questions.explanation: Both the butterfly's flying effect and the watering can's pouring effect work the same way: alternate between costumes with short waits in between, giving the illusion of continuous motion.

questions.question: Because the crane and the watering can are two completely different sprites in two different Scratch projects within this chapter, their scripts and costumes are unrelated to each other.
questions.explanation: This is true -- the crane/crab animation (Animation and Storytelling) and the watering can (Growing Digital Plants) are separate Scratch activities within the chapter, each with its own sprites, costumes and scripts, even though both use similar block types like movement and events.

questions.question: The book's Scratch screenshot shows blocks like 'broadcast message1', 'wait 1 seconds', 'repeat 10', and 'forever' in the Code tab. What does this tell you about how Scratch scripts are built?
options: Scripts can only ever use one block at a time
Scripts are built by snapping multiple different block types together into a sequence
Only the 'Motion' category can be used
Blocks cannot be combined with each other
questions.explanation: The screenshot shows blocks from different categories (Events, Control) stacked together, illustrating that a Scratch script is simply a combination of multiple blocks connected in sequence to produce a full behaviour.

questions.question: Besides the Code tab, which other tabs are visible in the Scratch interface shown in the book?
questions.explanation: The Scratch window in the book's screenshot shows three tabs: Code, Costumes, and Sounds -- Code is where you build scripts, Costumes lets you manage a sprite's looks, and Sounds manages audio.

questions.question: The Scratch interface has separate tabs for Code, Costumes, and Sounds.
questions.explanation: The screenshot in the book clearly shows these three tabs at the top of the sprite editing area: Code, Costumes, and Sounds.

questions.question: What is shown in the small panel at the bottom-right of the Scratch window, next to the sprite list?
options: The Stage's current backdrop thumbnail area
questions.explanation: The bottom-right area of the Scratch window shows the 'Backdrops' section with a thumbnail, separate from the sprite list on the left which shows sprites like Crane and Sprite1.

questions.question: A student believes 'a Scratch project can only ever have ONE sprite.' Why is this incorrect?
options: This chapter's own projects use multiple sprites together, e.g. crane + crab, and plant + watering can + butterfly
Scratch requires exactly 2 sprites, never more or fewer
Sprites are not allowed in Scratch at all
questions.explanation: Multiple sprites working together is central to this chapter: the animation project needs both a crane and a crab sprite, and the garden project needs a plant, a watering can, and a butterfly sprite all interacting via broadcast messages.

questions.question: Which of these is an accurate one-sentence description of what this ICT chapter teaches, based on its own introduction?
options: How to make characters of a story move and much more with Scratch
How to write a crossword puzzle from scratch (paper only)
How to play a musical instrument
questions.explanation: The chapter's own 'Get Set, Go!' introduction ends with: 'Let us learn how to make characters of a story move and much more with Scratch!'

questions.question: Why do you think this chapter chose Scratch specifically to teach BOTH animation and fractions, instead of two separate unrelated tools?
options: Because Scratch happens to be the only software that exists
Because Scratch's visual, block-based approach lets young learners build movement, drawing, and logic (like conditions and variables) all in the same simple environment
Because fractions and animation are the same thing
There is no reason, it is random
questions.explanation: Scratch's drag-and-drop blocks make it accessible for beginners to build many different kinds of projects -- movement/animation, pen-tool drawing for fractions, and logic with variables for the plant simulation -- all using the same simple block-based interface.

questions.question: In the book's loop example, 'repeat 10: move 50 steps, turn 180 degrees' is contrasted with 'forever: move 10 steps, turn 20 degrees.' What is different about the step/degree values used in each example?
options: They are identical in both examples
The repeat example uses bigger movement (50 steps, 180 degrees) while the forever example uses smaller, continuous movement (10 steps, 20 degrees)
The forever example uses negative numbers
Only the repeat example uses degrees
questions.explanation: The book's repeat example uses larger values (50 steps, 180 degrees turn) suited to a fixed number of big back-and-forth movements, while the forever example uses smaller values (10 steps, 20 degrees) suited to smooth, continuous background motion.

questions.question: If you wanted your crab sprite to flip and face the opposite direction, which block would you most likely use?
questions.explanation: Turning 180 degrees flips a sprite to face the opposite direction it was previously facing -- this is a common use of the 'turn degrees' block.

questions.question: The 'move steps' block changes the direction a sprite is facing.
questions.explanation: This is false -- 'move steps' moves the sprite FORWARD in whatever direction it is currently facing; it is the 'turn degrees' block that changes the facing direction.

questions.question: A crab sprite is facing right (direction 90) and its script says 'move 50 steps' with no turn block before it. Which way will the crab move?
options: To the right, since it moves in whatever direction it is currently facing
It will not move at all
questions.explanation: Since 'move steps' always moves a sprite forward in its CURRENT facing direction, and the crab is facing right (direction 90), it will move to the right across the stage.

questions.question: Which pair of blocks together let you make a crane 'glide smoothly to a new spot while also facing the right way'?
questions.explanation: 'glide' smoothly animates the sprite to a new position over time, and 'point in direction' ensures it faces the correct way while doing so -- together giving natural-looking movement, like a crane flying over a lake.

questions.question: Which of these blocks would you use to make a sprite look at another sprite on the other side of the stage?
questions.explanation: The 'turn degrees' block changes which way a sprite is facing, which the book specifically notes is useful to 'make characters look at each other in your animations.'

questions.question: A student wants a crane to 'say I'm hungry' only AFTER it has finished moving to its spot, not before. What sequencing choice makes this happen?
options: Placing the 'say' block anywhere at random in the stack
Placing the 'move'/'go to' block ABOVE the 'say' block in the same script, so movement finishes first
questions.explanation: Since Scratch runs a stack of blocks top to bottom in order, placing the movement block above the 'say' block ensures the crane finishes moving before it says 'I'm hungry!'.

questions.question: In Scratch, the exact order in which you stack blocks does not affect what happens when the script runs.
questions.explanation: This is false -- Scratch executes stacked blocks strictly in the order they appear, from top to bottom, so changing the order can completely change the animation's result.

questions.question: What everyday activity does the book compare 'sequencing' to?
options: Cooking a meal with no instructions
Reading a story from beginning to end
Watching TV with the sound off
questions.explanation: The book directly compares sequencing to 'reading a story from beginning to end' -- both involve following steps or events in a fixed, meaningful order.

questions.question: Which loop block would best suit 'keep checking the plant's water and sunlight levels until it finally reaches the mature stage, however long that takes'?
questions.explanation: 'repeat until' is exactly designed for this: it keeps looping (checking conditions) until a specific condition -- here growth stage = 4 -- becomes true, then it stops automatically, unlike 'forever' which never stops and 'repeat 10' which stops after a fixed count regardless of the plant's actual state.

questions.question: Which of these are examples of loop blocks used in this chapter? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: repeat, forever, and repeat until are all loop blocks used across the chapter's projects. 'point in direction' is a motion block, not a loop.

questions.question: Why are loops described as helpful for avoiding 'repetitive coding'?
options: Because they let you write an action once and have it run multiple times, instead of copying the same blocks over and over
Because they delete extra blocks automatically
Because they only work with one block at a time
Because they change the backdrop automatically
questions.explanation: Loops let you place an action's blocks once inside a loop block (like 'repeat' or 'forever'), and Scratch automatically runs that action multiple times, saving you from copying and pasting the same blocks repeatedly.

questions.question: If a 'repeat until growth stage = 4' loop is running, and the growth stage variable becomes 4 partway through one pass of the loop's blocks, what generally happens?
options: The loop stops the very next time it checks the condition (typically at the start of its next pass)
The loop keeps running forever regardless
The loop deletes the growth stage variable
Nothing happens until the green flag is clicked again
questions.explanation: A 'repeat until' loop checks its condition at the top of each pass; once growth stage becomes 4, the NEXT time the loop checks the condition, it will stop repeating, since the condition (growth stage = 4) is now true.

questions.question: Why would using a 'repeat 4' loop (rather than 'repeat until') be the WRONG choice for managing the plant's growth stages?
options: Because 'repeat 4' is not a real Scratch block

Because 'repeat 4' would only run its actions exactly 4 times total and then stop, even if the plant hasn't actually reached the mature stage yet -- growth depends on water/sunlight conditions, not a fixed count
Because 'repeat 4' can only be used with fractions
There is no difference between the two
questions.explanation: Growth should depend on whether the plant HAS received enough water and sunlight at each stage, which can take a varying, unpredictable amount of checking -- a fixed 'repeat 4' would stop checking after 4 passes regardless of the plant's actual condition, which is why 'repeat until growth stage = 4' (condition-based) is the correct choice instead.

questions.question: Loops in Scratch repeat actions automatically, which saves time compared to writing the same blocks over and over.
questions.explanation: This matches the book directly: 'Loops in Scratch repeat actions automatically... They save time by avoiding repetitive coding.'

questions.question: What is the difference between a plain 'broadcast [message]' block and a 'broadcast [message] and wait' block?
options: 'broadcast and wait' pauses the sending sprite's script until all receiving scripts finish responding, while plain 'broadcast' does not wait
'broadcast and wait' sends the message to more sprites
'broadcast and wait' is used only for fractions
questions.explanation: 'broadcast [message] and wait' (seen in the plant's 'broadcast plant mature and wait' block) pauses the sender's own script until every sprite that received the message finishes its response, whereas a plain 'broadcast' block fires the message and immediately continues without waiting.

questions.question: Which sprite in the digital garden receives the 'plant mature' message?
questions.explanation: The butterfly sprite is programmed to receive the 'plant mature' broadcast message, which is its cue to appear and start flying around.

questions.question: A single broadcast message, like 'plant mature', can be received by more than one sprite at the same time if more than one sprite is listening for it.
questions.explanation: Broadcast messages in Scratch are heard by ALL sprites that have a matching 'when I receive' block -- so if multiple sprites listen for 'plant mature', all of them would respond, not just one.
questions.source: book:page18 (MILESTONE Section A Q5, extended reasoning)

questions.question: If the butterfly sprite's 'when I receive plant mature' block were accidentally deleted, what would happen when the plant becomes mature?
options: The plant would fail to become mature
The plant would still broadcast 'plant mature' as normal, but the butterfly would never respond or appear, since it no longer has a script listening for that message
The watering can would appear instead of the butterfly
Scratch would refuse to run the whole project
questions.explanation: Broadcasting a message doesn't depend on who's listening -- the plant would still successfully broadcast 'plant mature'. But without a 'when I receive plant mature' script, the butterfly sprite has no instructions telling it to appear, so it simply would not respond.

questions.question: What does the 'when I receive [message]' block do?
options: Sends a new message to all sprites
Starts running its attached blocks whenever the matching broadcast message is received
Waters the plant automatically every second
questions.explanation: 'when I receive [message]' is the receiving half of the broadcast system -- it runs its attached script only when the matching message has been broadcast by any sprite.

questions.question: Why might a Scratch project use different backdrops for different scenes, like a beach for the crane-and-crab story?
options: Backdrops have no real purpose in Scratch
Different backdrops set the right setting for each part of the story, making scene changes feel natural, especially when paired with 'go to' for quick transitions
Only one backdrop is ever allowed per project
Backdrops replace the need for sprites
questions.explanation: Custom backdrops let a story change settings (like moving between different lake scenes for a flying crane), and pairing backdrop changes with quick 'go to' movements creates natural-feeling scene transitions.

questions.question: In this chapter's animated story, why do the crane and crab both need their OWN separate movement blocks rather than sharing one set?
options: Because Scratch does not allow sharing anyway, and each sprite must be independently told what to do
Because only the crane is allowed to move
Because the crab does not need any blocks at all
Because sharing blocks would erase the pen tool drawings
questions.explanation: Each sprite in Scratch has its own independent script area; you must give each character (crane and crab) its own movement blocks so both can act -- one sprite's blocks do not automatically apply to another sprite.

questions.question: Timing the crane's and crab's actions carefully is important so their interactions in the story make sense.
questions.explanation: The book states that when adding multiple characters, 'we can make them interact with each other by timing their actions carefully' -- good timing is what makes multi-character animations look coordinated rather than random.

questions.question: What real-life idea does customizing backdrops in Scratch connect to?
options: Changing the setting or scene of a story, like moving from one place to another
questions.explanation: Backdrops represent the setting of a scene -- customizing them mirrors how a real story's setting can change from one place (like a lake) to another as the plot moves along.

questions.question: Why must you use 'erase all' before starting a new pen-tool drawing in Scratch?
options: It is not actually necessary and does nothing
So old pen drawings from a previous run don't remain mixed in with the new shape you are about to draw
It stops the loop from running
questions.explanation: 'Erase all' clears any previously drawn pen marks on the stage, ensuring your new fraction shape is drawn cleanly without leftover lines from earlier runs of the project.

questions.question: What is the purpose of 'set pen size' before drawing a fraction shape?
options: To control how thick or thin the drawn lines will be
To control how many loops run
questions.explanation: 'set pen size' controls the thickness of the lines the pen draws -- useful for making shape outlines and division lines clear and easy to see.

questions.question: To draw a shape with the pen tool where the drawing follows the sprite as it moves, which block must be turned on BEFORE the movement blocks run?
questions.explanation: 'pen down' must be active before the sprite moves so that the pen actually leaves a trail as the sprite travels; 'pen up' does the opposite and lifts the pen so movement leaves no mark -- useful for repositioning without drawing.
