questions.question: Which of the following steps, in this general order, would correctly draw a clean square divided visibly using the pen tool? (Select all that apply, regardless of order)
options: Set pen colour and pen size
questions.explanation: All four steps are genuinely part of the book's pen-tool square-drawing process: clear old drawings (erase all), choose colour/thickness (set pen colour/size), lower the pen so it draws (pen down), then repeat the move+turn sequence 4 times to trace a square's 4 equal sides.

questions.question: What number of equal parts would a shape have if it is divided to show the fraction 1/2?
options: 2 equal parts, with 1 of them representing the fraction
questions.explanation: The fraction 1/2 means 1 part out of 2 equal parts of a whole -- so the shape would be divided into 2 equal parts total.

questions.question: Comparing 1/2 and 3/4, which fraction represents a LARGER coloured portion of an equally divided shape?
questions.explanation: 3/4 (three out of four equal parts) is a larger portion than 1/2 (one out of two equal parts, i.e. half) -- 3/4 is greater than 1/2 when comparing fractions of the same whole.

questions.question: The pen tool in Scratch can be used to draw both squares and circles to show fractions.
questions.explanation: The book shows both a square example (repeat 4: move 100 steps, turn 90 degrees) and circle/pizza-slice examples for showing fractions -- so both shapes are used with the pen tool.

questions.question: In the mature-stage check, the book uses TWO nested if-then blocks: an outer one checking 'water level > 60 and sunlight hours > 30' and an inner one checking 'growth stage = 3'. Why use two separate checks instead of one big condition?
options: Scratch does not allow combining more than one comparison with 'and'
It is simply how the book chose to organize the logic -- both conditions must be true together for the plant to advance, whether combined into one 'and' or nested as two if-thens
The inner check is not actually needed at all
Because growth stage never actually reaches 3
questions.explanation: Functionally, both the water/sunlight condition AND the growth-stage condition must be true for the plant to advance to mature; the book nests them as two if-then blocks, but the same idea could also be written as one combined 'and' condition -- either way, ALL conditions must hold true together.

questions.question: Which growth stage number corresponds to the 'young plant' stage, based on the mature-stage check requiring 'growth stage = 3'?
questions.explanation: Since the check for becoming mature requires 'growth stage = 3' (meaning the plant is currently a young plant) before switching to growth stage 4 (mature), growth stage 3 corresponds to 'young plant'.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly matches a growth stage NUMBER to its name, based on the standard order seed(1)->sprout(2)->young plant(3)->mature(4)? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: Following the confirmed order (seed, sprout, young plant, mature), growth stage 1 = seed, 2 = sprout, 3 = young plant, and 4 = mature. It is FALSE that growth stage 3 = mature -- stage 3 is young plant, and stage 4 is mature.

questions.question: What does 'plant age' most likely track in the digital plant simulation?
options: How long (in time) the digital plant has existed or been growing
questions.explanation: 'Plant age' is one of the three variables shown alongside water level and sunlight hours, and -- as its name suggests -- it tracks how long the plant has existed/been growing over time.

questions.question: The digital plant's growth-stage advancement depends only on the water level, never on sunlight hours.
questions.explanation: This is false -- every growth-stage transition (seed->sprout, sprout->young, young->mature) requires BOTH enough water AND enough sunlight hours, not water alone.

questions.question: Suppose a plant has water level = 25 and sunlight hours = 8. Has it met the requirement to grow from seed to sprout (20 water / 10 sunlight)?
options: No -- water level (25) meets the requirement, but sunlight hours (8) is still below the required 10, so BOTH conditions are not yet true
No, because water level is too low
Yes, because water level is more than enough
questions.explanation: The seed-to-sprout transition requires water level > 20-ish threshold AND sunlight hours > 10-ish threshold together (the book's stated needs are 20 water/10 sunlight). Water (25) clears its requirement, but sunlight (8) is still below 10, so the overall condition (both must be true) is not yet satisfied.

questions.question: Both wilting and overwatering are described as plant 'problems.' What is the key difference between their causes?
options: They have the exact same cause
Wilting is caused by TOO LITTLE water (below 5), while overwatering is caused by TOO MUCH water (above 100)
Wilting is caused by too much sunlight, overwatering by too little sunlight
Neither is related to water at all
questions.explanation: Wilting and overwatering are opposite problems: wilting happens when water level drops below 5 (too little), while overwatering happens when water level rises above 100 (too much) -- both are avoidable by keeping water in a healthy middle range.

questions.question: According to the worksheet, if your digital plant is wilting, what should you do?
options: Click on the watering can sprite to increase the water level
Wait for the butterfly to appear
questions.explanation: The worksheet's own fill-in-the-blank instruction is: click on the watering can sprite to increase the water level variable when the plant is wilting.

questions.question: A student clicks the watering can sprite 20 times in a row without checking the water level. What risk does this create?
options: No risk at all, more water is always better
A risk of overwatering, since water level could rise above 100 and make the plant look yellow and sick
A risk that the plant will instantly become a butterfly
A risk that the crossword puzzle will disappear
questions.explanation: Since overwatering triggers once water level goes above 100, repeatedly clicking the watering can without checking the current level risks pushing water level too high, causing the plant to become yellow and sick ('Too much water! I'm drowning!').

questions.question: Which of these are legitimate ways to influence the digital plant's variables, according to the book's blocks? (Select all that apply)
options: Clicking the watering can sprite (raises water level)
Pressing the 'S' key (raises sunlight hours by 10)
Waiting for the butterfly to lower the water level
questions.explanation: Only clicking the watering can (raising water level) and pressing 'S' (raising sunlight hours by 10) are shown as real ways to influence the plant's variables. There is no crossword-click or butterfly action that changes water/sunlight in this project.

questions.question: What message does the plant say when the watering can sprite waters it and gives it just the right amount over time (no wilting, no overwatering)?
options: There is no special message for balanced care -- the plant simply continues growing normally toward its next stage
questions.explanation: The book only shows special messages for the PROBLEM states (wilting: 'I'm wilting! Need water!'; overwatering: 'Too much water! I'm drowning!') and the success state (mature: 'I'm fully grown!'). Balanced, in-between care has no special complaint message -- the plant simply keeps progressing normally.

questions.question: Why does the book emphasize 'balance' when discussing plant care rather than simply saying 'give as much water and sunlight as possible'?
options: Because more is always better with no limit
Because giving too much water causes overwatering (yellow, sick plant), so care must stay within a healthy range, not just maximized
Because sunlight has no effect on the plant at all
Because balance only matters for fractions, not plants
questions.explanation: The book explicitly warns that overwatering (too much water) is just as harmful as wilting (too little water) -- so care must be balanced within a healthy range rather than simply maximized.

questions.question: Which comes FIRST in the digital garden's sequence of events: the plant reaching growth stage 4, or the butterfly appearing?
options: The butterfly appears first, then the plant matures
The plant reaches growth stage 4 (mature) first, which then broadcasts a message that makes the butterfly appear
They always happen at exactly the same instant with no dependency
Neither is connected to the other
questions.explanation: The order is: the plant meets its water/sunlight conditions, advances to growth stage 4 (mature), broadcasts 'plant mature' -- and only THEN does the butterfly, upon receiving that message, appear and start flying.

questions.question: The butterfly's role in the digital garden is purely decorative and has no connection to how well the plant has been cared for.
questions.explanation: This is false -- the butterfly's appearance is directly tied to plant care: it only shows up after the plant successfully reaches the mature stage (i.e. after being watered and given sunlight correctly), so it reflects good care, not random decoration.

questions.question: What does the presence of a butterfly in the digital garden suggest about the plant?
options: The plant has grown flowers and reached the mature stage
The plant has just been planted as a seed
questions.explanation: Since the butterfly only appears after receiving the 'plant mature' broadcast, seeing the butterfly signals that the plant has successfully grown flowers and reached the mature stage.

questions.question: Why is it meaningful, from a real-life-connection point of view, that the butterfly only appears once the plant is mature and has flowers?
options: It isn't meaningful at all, it's arbitrary
It mirrors real life, where butterflies are attracted to flowering plants rather than seeds or bare soil
Because butterflies only like watering cans
questions.explanation: In real gardens, butterflies are drawn to flowers for nectar, not to seeds or bare soil -- the simulation's rule (butterfly appears only once the plant flowers/matures) reflects this real-world behaviour.

questions.question: What does the book suggest about making the garden simulation 'more interactive'?
options: Adding more creatures or responses, like the butterfly, that react to the plant's condition
questions.explanation: The book poses the reflective question 'How would you make your garden more interactive?' right after discussing communication via messages -- implying that adding more responsive elements (like more creatures reacting to plant state) increases interactivity.

questions.question: The chapter includes TWO separate review crossword puzzles -- one in a worksheet and one on a book review page. Which set of words belongs to the WORKSHEET crossword (Animation, Integration, Transition, Fractions, Loop)?
options: None of the words appear in either crossword
questions.explanation: The worksheet crossword's answers are Animation, Integration, Fractions (across) and Transition, Loop (down) -- this is a different puzzle from the book's own review-page crossword, which instead uses Sprites, Butterfly, Variables, Coordination, and Sequencing.
questions.source: book:page54 (worksheet crossword, distinguishing from book review crossword)

questions.question: Which word would best fit the clue 'A digital puppet you can control in Scratch' in a crossword?
questions.explanation: A 'sprite' is exactly this: a digital puppet/character in Scratch that you control using code blocks.

questions.question: Two crossword clues in this chapter both relate to timing/order: one says 'the smooth change from one stage to another' (Transition) and another says 'putting movement blocks in the right order' (Sequencing). What is the key difference between these two ideas?
options: They are exactly the same idea with two different names
'Transition' describes changing FROM one stage/state TO another (like sprout to young plant), while 'Sequencing' describes the ORDER of individual instructions within one sprite's script
questions.explanation: 'Transition' is about moving between overall states or stages (e.g. a plant's growth stage changing, or a scene changing), while 'Sequencing' is specifically about the order in which individual blocks/instructions run within a script -- related but distinct ideas.

questions.question: Considering the whole chapter, which single Scratch feature is used in ALL THREE major projects (crane/crab animation, fraction drawing, and digital plant)?
questions.explanation: Every project in this chapter -- the crane/crab story, the fraction-drawing activity, and the digital plant simulation -- relies on sprites controlled by their own block-based scripts, even though each project uses different specific blocks.

questions.question: Which of these correctly distinguish 'variables' from 'sprites' in Scratch, based on this chapter? (Select all that apply)
options: A sprite is a character/digital puppet on the stage, like the crane or the plant
A variable is a stored piece of information, like water level or growth stage, that can change over time
Variables and sprites are the exact same thing
A single sprite's script can check and change variable values using if-then and 'set variable' blocks
questions.explanation: Sprites are characters on the stage, while variables are stored data values that scripts can read and change (e.g. the plant's script checks and sets water level, sunlight hours, growth stage). They are NOT the same thing -- one is a visible character, the other is invisible stored information.

questions.question: Which topic in this chapter is most directly connected to mathematics (specifically parts of a whole)?
questions.explanation: 'Fractions Come Alive with Technology' is the sub-topic directly tied to the math concept of parts of a whole, taught here using Scratch's pen tool to draw and colour shapes.

questions.question: Which of these projects in the chapter relies MOST heavily on variables and conditional (if-then) logic?
questions.explanation: The digital plant simulation is the most logic-heavy project: it uses several variables (water level, sunlight hours, plant age, growth stage) and if-then/repeat-until conditions to decide when the plant grows, wilts, or becomes overwatered.

questions.question: This chapter, 'The Learning Web', uses the Scratch program to connect coding with storytelling, math (fractions), and simulating real-life plant care.
questions.explanation: This summarizes the chapter accurately: Scratch is used across three connected activities -- animating a story, visualizing fractions, and simulating digital plant growth/care -- all in one program.
